title: 7: t-tests
text:
Correct answer: No
Explanation: A normal distribution is a specific function that has exact values. While this function might describe the general shape of real world phenomenon, it does not perfectly reflect real world mechanisms for generating data. One property of a normal distribution is that the tails go on to infinity. This is not a property of most real world phenomenon. Real world data never perfectly match hypothetical functions that we define.

title: 7: t-tests
text:
Do you think samples are drawn from a population that approximates a normal distribution?

Likely
Unlikely

title: 7: t-tests
text:
Correct answer: Likely
Explanation: The general shape of each frequency polygon appears to have a mean with more or less even spread around it. They are not really skewed (notice that any extension of lines are actually at count = 0). This seems reasonable because one expects that there is a central tendency that most people agree upon, and deviations from the mean comes from random “errors” that are not systematically biased, like ambiguity of the rating scale, variations in personality, mood, etc. Generally, if a research question concerns means, you can expect what gets measured will be more or less normally distributed.

People have higher levels of fear for flying than for driving. The peaks of the frequency polygons are offset quite noticeably with very little overlap, suggesting that the difference likely generalizes to the true population as well as future samples.
In this particular dataset, there is a difference in mean ratings between the driving a flying conditions. However, we cannot conclude if this difference is generalizable to the true population or any future samples.
We cannot form any conclusions from this plot alone. Even though the peaks look different, we have not plotted the confidence intervals. Therefore, we cannot be sure about the difference in means for this experiment, and by extension, the true population.

By subtracting the line from the individual data points, the slope and intercept are “removed”, and all that is left is the noise from individuals. In other words, all that is left are the errors. If the model is the true model, then the true errors are random (by definition, errors are random). The “errors” that a model predicts are the called the residuals.


\(y_\text{model} = \text{intercept}_\text{model} + \text{slope}_\text{model} \times x_\text{data points}\)
\(y_\text{data points} =  y_\text{model} + \text{errors}_\text{model}\)
\(\text{errors}_\text{model} = y_\text{data points} - y_\text{model}\)
